t: F and J have bumps for a reason
b: The small ridges on the F and J keys let touch typists find the home row without looking. Your index fingers rest there, and the other fingers fall into place along the row.

q.p: Why do the F and J keys have bumps?
o: To find the home row by touch

rq.p: Which fingers rest on F and J?

why: Touch typing relies on feel, not sight.

b: For years, many reCAPTCHA puzzles showed two words: one the system knew, and one scanned from an old book that computers couldn't read. By typing both, millions of people helped digitise books and newspapers.

q.p: What did typing reCAPTCHA words once help do?

rq.p: How did reCAPTCHA know you were human?
o: You typed the known word right
It checked your typing speed only

why: It turned a security check into useful work.

t: The internet runs under the sea
b: The vast majority of data travelling between continents goes through fibre-optic cables on the seabed, not satellites. Hundreds of these cables crisscross the oceans, some thinner than a garden hose.

q.p: How does most internet data cross oceans?

rq.p: What do undersea internet cables carry data with?

why: Cables carry far more data, faster and cheaper, than satellites.

b: When you send a photo, it's chopped into thousands of small packets. Each packet may take a different route across the internet, and your friend's device puts them back in order. Lost packets are simply re-sent.

q.p: How does a photo travel across the internet?

rq.p: What happens to a lost packet?

why: Small packets share network links efficiently.

b: Every pixel on your screen is made of tiny red, green and blue parts. By mixing their brightness, a screen can create millions of colours. Look at a screen with a magnifying glass and you can see the separate dots.

q.p: Which three colours make every colour on your screen?

rq.p: How do screens make yellow?

why: Your eye has three types of colour receptors.

b: Studies show prices ending in .99 make people feel something is noticeably cheaper than the round number. We read left to right, so £9.99 registers as 'nine-something'. It's called the left-digit effect.

q.p: Why do shops price things at £9.99?
o: The first digit sways our sense of price

rq.p: What's this effect called?

why: We judge numbers quickly by their first digit.

t: Many crossing buttons once did nothing
b: In 2004, The New York Times reported that most of New York's pedestrian crossing buttons no longer worked, because the lights ran on timers. Many cities still keep some buttons only for daytime or night-time use.

q.p: What did a 2004 report find about New York crossing buttons?

rq.p: Why didn't the buttons work?

why: Computerised traffic timing replaced on-demand crossings.

b: Earth takes about 365.2422 days to go round the Sun. Adding a leap day every four years overcorrects slightly, so century years skip it unless divisible by 400. 2000 was a leap year; 1900 wasn't, and 2100 won't be.

q.p: Will 2100 be a leap year?

rq.p: Why was 2000 a leap year?

why: The rule keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons.

t: China uses a single time zone
b: China spans about five geographical time zones but uses one official time, Beijing Time. In the far west, sunrise in winter can come after 9 a.m., and some people there unofficially use a local time two hours behind.

q.p: How many official time zones does China use?

rq.p: What happens in China's far west because of this?

why: A single zone was adopted in 1949 for national unity.

b: Germany and Austria-Hungary were the first to adopt daylight saving time nationally, in 1916, to save fuel for the war effort. Britain followed a few weeks later with British Summer Time.

q.p: Which country first adopted daylight saving nationally?

rq.p: Why was daylight saving first introduced?

why: An extra hour of evening daylight cut lighting costs.

b: Since 1967, one second has been officially defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium-133 atom. Atomic clocks count these and are so precise they would drift by less than a second over millions of years.

q.p: What defines one official second?

rq.p: When was this definition adopted?

why: Atoms are more regular than Earth's slightly wobbly spin.

b: We split hours into 60 minutes and circles into 360 degrees thanks to the ancient Babylonians, who counted in base 60. Sixty divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30.

q.p: Why are there 60 minutes in an hour?

rq.p: Why is 60 a handy number?
o: It divides evenly in many ways

why: Easy division made trade and astronomy simpler.

t: Most fund managers don't beat the market
b: Each year, S&P's SPIVA reports compare active investment funds with simple index funds that track a whole market. Over 10 to 15 years, the large majority of active funds do worse than their index, partly due to higher fees.

q.p: Over 15 years, do most active funds beat a simple index?

rq.p: What's one big reason active funds lag?

why: Small yearly fees compound into large differences.

b: Bitcoin's code limits the total supply to 21 million coins. New coins are released ever more slowly, halving the reward roughly every four years, with the last fractions expected around the year 2140.

q.p: What's the maximum number of bitcoins that can exist?

rq.p: How often does the new-bitcoin reward halve?

why: A fixed supply was a design choice by its creator.

b: A night's sleep moves through repeating cycles of lighter, deeper and dreaming (REM) sleep, each roughly 90 minutes. Deep sleep dominates early in the night, while REM periods get longer toward morning.

q.p: Roughly how long is one sleep cycle?

rq.p: When do dreaming (REM) periods get longest?

why: The brain cycles through different restorative stages.

b: Many parents believe sugar makes kids hyperactive, but controlled studies, including a 1995 analysis of many trials, found no real effect on behaviour. In one study, parents told their child had sugar rated them more hyper, even when it was a placebo.

q.p: Does sugar make children hyperactive?

rq.p: What did parents do when told their child had sugar?

why: Expectation shapes what we see.

b: The pop comes from gas bubbles forming in the fluid of the joint. Doctor Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of only one hand for over 60 years and found no arthritis difference between hands. Larger studies agree.

q.p: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?

rq.p: What makes the knuckle pop?

why: Unger won an Ig Nobel Prize for his one-man experiment.

t: Muscle memory lives in your brain
b: When you learn to ride a bike or type, the 'muscle memory' is stored in the brain, in areas like the cerebellum and motor cortex, not in the muscles themselves. Practice makes the brain's control of movement faster and more automatic.

q.p: Where is 'muscle memory' actually stored?

rq.p: Which brain area helps fine-tune movements?

why: Repetition strengthens the brain circuits controlling a skill.

t: Habits take about two months to form
b: A 2009 UCL study tracked people building a new daily habit. On average it took about 66 days for the behaviour to feel automatic, but individuals ranged widely from 18 to 254 days. Missing a day now and then didn't ruin progress.

q.p: On average, how long did a new habit take to feel automatic?

rq.p: Did missing one day derail habit-building?

why: Consistency over weeks matters more than perfection.

b: When you 'multitask' on mental tasks, your brain usually switches rapidly between them. Each switch costs time and attention, so doing two demanding things at once is often slower and more error-prone than doing them one after another.

q.p: What does the brain mostly do when 'multitasking'?

rq.p: What's the cost of switching tasks?

why: Attention can only fully focus on one demanding task.

b: Your tongue detects only basic tastes like sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. The rich flavours of food come mostly from smell, as aromas travel up the back of your throat. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose.

q.p: Why does food taste bland when you have a cold?
o: Your sense of smell is blocked

rq.p: Where do most food flavours come from?

why: Aromas reach your nose from inside your mouth.

b: Decaffeination removes most but not all caffeine. A cup of decaf coffee typically still has a few milligrams, compared with around 70 to 140 mg in a regular cup.

q.p: Does decaf coffee contain caffeine?

rq.p: About how much caffeine is in regular coffee?

why: Removing every last molecule would ruin the flavour.

b: In a pint of Guinness, bubbles near the glass wall drift downward. Scientists showed the bubbles rise in the middle, pushing liquid up, while liquid near the walls flows down, dragging bubbles with it.

q.p: Which way do bubbles near the glass travel in Guinness?

rq.p: What drags the bubbles down?
o: Liquid flowing down near the walls

why: Rising bubbles in the centre create a circulating current.

t: Mentos make cola erupt by roughness
b: Mentos sweets are covered in microscopic pits. Dropped into fizzy drink, these give dissolved carbon dioxide countless spots to form bubbles all at once. The sudden burst of gas launches a foaming fountain.

q.p: Why does a Mentos make cola erupt?

rq.p: What gas forms the fountain?

why: Bubbles need 'nucleation sites' to start forming.

t: The Leaning Tower leaned from the start
b: Construction of Pisa's bell tower began in 1173, and it started to lean during building because the soft ground on one side couldn't support it. Engineers straightened its tilt slightly between 1990 and 2001 to stop it falling.

q.p: When did the Leaning Tower of Pisa start leaning?

rq.p: What caused the lean?

why: Building took nearly 200 years; long pauses let the soil settle.
